cv_interview_alignment.summary: Daniel's CV claims 'custom vector database' and 'multi-agent platform from scratch,' but the interview reveals he was not directly involved in low-level index tuning or the core infrastructure decisions. For a Senior AI Engineer at a startup, where hands-on technical depth is paramount, this gap between claimed and demonstrated expertise is the most critical issue.

project_suggestions.title: Build a minimal vector database from scratch
project_suggestions.why: Addresses the gap between claiming 'custom vector database' and actually understanding indexing internals. Demonstrates hands-on ability to implement HNSW or IVF, handle multi-modal embeddings, and benchmark latency.
project_suggestions.outcome: You can say: 'I implemented a vector index from scratch using HNSW, achieving sub-10ms recall on 1M vectors, and integrated it with CLIP embeddings for cross-modal retrieval.'

project_suggestions.title: Contribute to an open-source multi-agent framework (e.g., AutoGen, CrewAI)
project_suggestions.why: Demonstrates deep understanding of agent orchestration patterns, routing protocols, and failure modes—areas where the interview revealed gaps. A PR that adds a new handoff protocol or observability feature would be highly credible.
project_suggestions.outcome: You can say: 'I contributed a contract-net routing protocol to AutoGen, which improved handoff reliability in multi-agent systems by 30%.'

project_suggestions.title: Write a detailed technical blog post on multi-agent orchestration patterns
project_suggestions.why: Forces you to articulate the trade-offs between different patterns (orchestrator-worker vs. swarm vs. hierarchical) and share concrete lessons from your Nexus AI experience. This builds credibility and shows you can communicate technical depth.

interview_tips.observation: When asked about the custom vector database, Daniel said 'we used a standard HNSW-type indexing approach' and admitted he wasn't involved in low-level tuning. This undermines the CV claim of building a custom solution.
interview_tips.suggestion: If you weren't directly involved in implementation, reframe your contribution honestly: 'I architected the overall RAG pipeline and selected HNSW as the indexing strategy, while the infra team handled the low-level tuning.' Then pivot to what you did own.

interview_tips.observation: Daniel's answers about the multi-agent platform stayed at a high level ('balancing latency with accuracy') without breaking down the specific routing algorithm or failure modes.
interview_tips.suggestion: Use the STAR-L structure: Situation, Task, Action, Result, and then a specific Lesson learned. For example: 'The routing algorithm was a weighted classifier that considered query complexity and model latency. The biggest failure was when two similar queries got routed differently—we added a confidence threshold to catch borderline cases.'

interview_tips.observation: Daniel consistently used 'we' and credited the team, which is good for humility but makes it hard for the interviewer to assess his individual contribution.
interview_tips.suggestion: When asked about a project, start with the team context, then explicitly state: 'My personal contribution was X. I made the decision to Y because of Z trade-off.' This shows ownership without diminishing the team.

interview_tips.observation: Daniel's tone is confident and enthusiastic, but when pressed on technical specifics, he becomes vague and uses filler phrases like 'mainly about' and 'honestly.'
interview_tips.suggestion: If you don't know a detail, it's better to say 'I don't recall the exact implementation, but the principle was...' rather than hedging. Confidence in admitting gaps is more credible than vague answers.
